correctness.rationale: The center must be homogeneous, yielding exactly two cases. Center-even gradings correspond bijectively to symplectic orthogonal V0+V1 with V1 dimension 2r and a functional V1→Z; orbit-stabilizer gives q^(2r) Sp2m/(Sp2r Sp2m-2r). Center-odd gradings correspond bijectively to ordered transverse Lagrangian pairs and a functional V0→Z; orbit-stabilizer yields q^m Sp2m/GLm. Symplectic automorphisms and central shears prove m+2 group orbits. Euler normalization yields q^(m²+m) times a bounded theta-series summation for even-center grades, whereas odd-center grades number q^(m²+2m) times an Euler product. Dominated convergence proves the relative rare-event constant and conditional total-variation law. Independent brute-force enumeration matches q=2 dimensions 3,5 and q=3 dimension 3; extrapolation is not used.

The accepted assertion counts all labeled Z2-gradings in every finite dimension over every Fq and derives a sharp growing-rank probability and conditional theta law. Neither the inspected 2014 full-text theorem/sections nor the inspected 2022 finite-field simple-Lie algorithm paper gives the finite counts or the parity-dependent probability asymptotics. Semantic literature-index searches for Heisenberg Z2 grading enumeration, symplectic orbit parameters and center-parity theta limits located related centralizer/subalgebra/automorphism studies but no dominating claim. A previous broad structure theorem may make portions derivable, so novelty is confined to the quantitatively assembled law and its proof.

value.rationale: It gives a complete exact census for a standard family of graded Lie algebras across every finite field and rank, including the characteristic-two case where involution-eigenspace heuristics fail. More significantly, it quantitatively shows that center-even gradings become exponentially rare with a field- and parity-dependent discrete-theta constant and a non-Gaussian conditional degree split; this is a natural invariant of random gradings, rather than an arbitrary finite slice. The symmetry-group count has transparent potential use as a benchmark for enumeration algorithms.
